Welcome to the 10th edition of the U-CAN newsletter!

I am pleased to share the 10th edition of the U-CAN newsletter. The month of August has been busy for U-CAN. We launched our open-to-public Policy Webinar series and conducted two webinars with highly experienced panelists — one on "Urban Systems and Governance", and the other on "Affordable Urban Housing". Secondly, we have elected three co-chairs who will be guiding us on our priority themes of work — WRI India (Gender), Praja (Community Engagement) and Artha Global (Economic Development). We thank them for taking the U-CAN leadership forward. We look forward to the traction through our continued conversations on all matters related to urban development in the second half of the year.

- Siddharth Pandit, CEO, U-CAN

U-CAN Initiatives

Urban Systems and Governance webinar: This webinar was conducted on 8 Aug, 2024 with Milind Mhaske, CEO, Praja Foundation, Anand Iyer, Chief Policy and Insights Officer, Janaagraha and Shishir Ranjan Dash, Lead - Urban Habitat, Tata Steel Foundation. The session attempted to uncover the complexities of Indian urban systems and the structures governing them.

Interesting insights (and call to action) that emerged from the discussion:

It is vital to put systems in place while cities are smaller, else the service delivery gaps will worsen as the cities grow. Therefore, focusing on Tier II and Tier shall be the priority Both the government and social sector have to go beyond solving the symptoms of the issues that lie in the governance and planning process of cities Collectives such as U-CAN can help scale up the convening and conversations for larger collaboration with government agencies for strategic planning as cities have been sporadic in their efforts to redress issues and been reactive to crises, whereas the need is for sustained systemic change Research shows having better representation in both municipal council and administration will help in improving the quality of spending and build infrastructure that is more responsive towards building public interest. Hence, it is essential for an increase in gender participation at all levels of municipal governance, especially the administration The urban ecosystem has the potential to proactively engage and work with donors to help establish an urban portfolio for longer term meaningful outcomes Affordable Urban Housing webinar: This webinar, organised on 23 August, 2024, attempted to examine the barriers to affordable housing, the root causes that sustain this crisis and the transformative potential of innovative approaches like affordable rental housing and community- driven design. Siddharth Pandit - CEO, Urban Collective Action Network discussed with Pritika Hingorani, CEO (India), Artha Global and Pratima Joshi, Founder and Executive Director, Shelter Associates.

Interesting insights (and call to action) that emerged from the discussion:

The availability of quality affordable housing is crucial for cities to sustain as engines of economic growth. The private sector struggles to address this need among households at the lower end of the income spectrum. Therefore, government intervention is imperative to address the housing shortage.

Making housing affordable will require a 'systems approach' that not only incentivizes the building of new houses, but also activates rental housing and integrates aspects of city-level economic and spatial planning, public transport, innovative financing, and provision of basic infrastructure and social amenities.

Better monitoring, coordination, grievance redressal, and accessibility of data among state authorities and ULBs are vital for overcoming implementation-level issues that result in delays and cost overruns.

Equipping ULB officials with granular data is crucial for enabling better urban housing design, planning, and implementation. Improved availability of gender-disaggregated data will ensure housing that responds to the specific needs of women.

Collaboration among policymakers and implementers is indispensable to addressing both macro and micro aspects of the urban housing problem.

The State of Women’s Representation in Urban Local Self-Government in India: A Review

27 Aug, 2024 The review explores the current landscape of women's participation in urban local governance in India, emphasizing the importance of their representation for inclusive and effective policymaking. It highlights both the progress made through gender quotas and social and institutional barriers that limit women’s political agency and effectiveness. The review calls for systemic changes and enhanced policies to empower women and ensure their meaningful participation in local governance.

Ongoing Struggle for Women’s Safety and Mobility in India’s Urban Spaces

22 Aug, 2024 The article is closely tied to one of U-CAN's focus areas - gender. The author, co-founder and CEO of Safetipin, details her experiences as a woman navigating the streets of Delhi, highlighting the everyday challenges women face in public spaces due to safety concerns. It underscores the systemic issues that make cities unfriendly for women, such as inadequate lighting and lack of safe public transport. The article calls for a reimagining of cities to be more inclusive, diverse, and respectful of women's rights to safety and dignity. U-CAN is also working closely with Satefipin for its upcoming fellowship for urban professionals.

Editor's Note

I’m excited to share some great news from U-CAN! Our very first cohort of mid-career professionals is set to kick off their Fellowship with us in October. This Fellowship offers a unique chance for those passionate about urban development to dive into hands-on work with our network of partner organisations over the next year. It’s an opportunity to gain real-world experience, receive valuable mentorship, and take part in projects that create real change on the ground. We believe this Fellowship is a key step in building the knowledge and skills needed to tackle the complex challenges facing our cities today. In this newsletter, we’ll also take a closer look at how capacity building can help overcome these challenges, and as always, we value your insights and collaboration as we work collectively to drive impactful urban development across our key focus areas.

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

U-CAN Initiatives

Through our Fellowship, we aim to engage talented women professionals in the urban development sector, offering them a platform to enhance their skills while actively contributing to the impactful work of our member organizations, ultimately strengthening the broader urban ecosystem.

The Importance of Urban Capacity Building

Many local governments struggle with staff shortages and lack the expertise to address these growing issues, and resource constraints only make it tougher. Capacity building improves governance by focusing on strengthening local governments' ability to manage urban challenges.

By adopting an intersectional lens, capacity building furthers systemic ways of thinking, looking at sectors such as infrastructure, social services and climate resilience together rather than in silos.

Over the years, there have been many government interventions on capacity building of urban local body officials, including the Capacity Building Scheme for ULBs and the most recently launched Mission Karamyogi. Building capacities in India’s cities is not just a challenge at the city-level, but also a priority to achieve progress on various national and state-level policies and programs.

Read More (Capacity Building Scheme for ULBs) →

Read More (Mission Karamyogi) →

Advancing Urban Governance: Strengthening City Leadership and Institutional Capacity

Such interventions have adopted different approaches towards a common goal of strengthening institutional and individual capacities of city officials. For example, the Government of India’s Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) has identified municipal or city- level capacity building as a focus area, and according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the initial target of providing capacity building training to 45,000 officials has been complete. Existing interventions, initiatives and programs from the government as well as from NGOs and the private sector have also contributed to furthering capacity building in various ways.

For example, this report underscores the importance of building institutional capacity and ensuring transparency to specifically maximize the effectiveness of PPPs and enhance service delivery in urban areas, while this issue brief on ‘City Leaders of Karnataka’ by U-CAN member Janaagraha presents an overview of the unique challenges faced by city leaders in Karnataka.

A Study to Qualitatively Assess the Capacity Building Needs of Urban Local Bodies - NITI Aayog

The report highlights the critical challenges faced by ULBs, including acute staff shortages, inadequate skills, and a lack of institutional frameworks to support continuous improvement.

The study underscores the need for governance reforms, capacity-building strategies, and better resource management to address these gaps and strengthen local urban governance.

Recommendations include creating municipal cadres, improving training programs, and enhancing collaboration between ULBs and state governments.

Mainstreaming Women-led Frameworks - Urban20 →

The report emphasises the need for integrating gender responsive strategies in urban development to create inclusive, sustainable, and equitable cities. It highlights the critical role of women in urban planning and governance, aiming to address gender inequalities through participation, leadership, and decision-making.

Key themes include recognising the importance of gender-disaggregated data, supporting environmentally responsible behaviors, and promoting women's economic empowerment.

Urban Planning for City Leaders - UN →

Habitat →

"Urban Planning for City Leaders" by UN-Habitat emphasises the importance of strategic urban planning for city leaders, particularly in rapidly growing intermediate cities in developing countries. It highlights that proper urban planning is crucial for addressing challenges like rapid population growth, environmental degradation, and infrastructure demands. By adopting integrated, cross-sector approaches and planning at a sufficient scale, city leaders can enhance urban governance, manage growth effectively, and promote sustainable development.

The index is based on four themes, 13 sub-themes and 42 indicators, which determine democratic and empowered functioning of urban governments.

Editor's Note

Continuing from the kick-off of the U-CAN Fellowship for mid-career professionals last month, I'm excited to share that we have expanded the cohort with our social entrepreneurs joining the Fellowship this month. We invited our shortlist of entrepreneurs to make a case for their work and be evaluated by a group comprising all our member organisations, making it a truly collective and collaborative effort! Interestingly, both our social entrepreneur fellows' work has a strong community engagement component, which is also the theme of this month's newsletter. In this edition, we'll take a look at how urban residents engage in their cities and the role of technology in enabling it. We highlight some successful initiatives from across the country here. We'd love to hear from you of any initiatives in your city, as we believe that with every story shared, we move a step closer to encouraging people to engage in their neighbourhoods and cities.

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

U-CAN Initiatives

U-CAN conducted an Innovation Showcase to evaluate the shortlisted candidates for the U-CAN Fellowship under the social entrepreneurs track, and are thrilled to have our social entrepreneur Fellows join us for our Fellowship! Their ventures tackle urban environment issues and neglect of historical heritage putting community engagement at the front and centre of their work.

Community Engagement in Urban Governance

Urban residents in India participate in shaping their environments through various channels. These include both individual and collective actions, where citizens take part in local activism or form neighbourhood associations to address urban issues like infrastructure and services. Institutional mechanisms like ward committees offer formal avenues for involvement, while digital platforms have emerged as powerful tools for organizing and voicing concerns. Additionally, partnerships with NGOs and civil society organizations help citizens engage in city planning and policy advocacy, amplifying the voices of marginalized groups. This spectrum of engagement reflects a growing desire among people to influence the future of their cities in meaningful ways. Read this article from the India Development Review to find out more.

Read More →

E-Governance and Citizen Engagement: Pathways to Resilient and Equitable Cities

The piece emphasizes the necessity of integrating e-governance with active citizen engagement to build resilient, inclusive urban environments. With insights from experts, it explores how digital public infrastructure, integrated transport systems, and smart city initiatives can streamline urban management, improve services, and foster sustainable development. The collection highlights the critical role of participatory governance, the challenges of digital divides, and the importance of local government autonomy and institutional reforms

Click on the image above to read more.

A Guide to Community Engagement for Public-Private Partnerships

The guide emphasises the importance of involving stakeholders throughout a project lifecycle. It outlines steps for effective communication, consultation, and collaboration with communities to enhance project success and social inclusion. Key methods include early stakeholder involvement, transparency in decision-making, and mechanisms for addressing community concerns.

Click on the image above to read more.

Playbook of Fostering Participatory Data Stewardship

The strategy emphasizes sustainability through open, interoperable data systems that enhance multi-stakeholder urban management. By encouraging public sector-led, standardized data- sharing infrastructures, it fosters efficient, secure, and accessible urban governance. This approach promotes sustainable urban development, bridging data gaps in crucial areas like air quality and geospatial mapping, empowering citizen-led initiatives and fostering innovation across sectors. The strategy’s focus on participatory design and accessible technology further enables community involvement, creating inclusive, resilient urban ecosystems.

Read More →

Suggested readings on Urban Capacity Building

Reviewing the Physical and Non-Physical Attributes of Collector and Local Streets: A Case Study of Mylapore, Chennai

The Mylapore case study in Chennai, India, highlights how urban street design affects community engagement. It examines the role of physical elements (like sidewalks, street width, and tree canopies) and non-physical elements (such as safety, imageability, and accessibility) in fostering social interaction, safety, and neighborhood identity. By creating pedestrian- friendly spaces and preserving heritage buildings, the study illustrates how thoughtful street planning can improve liveability, encouraging more community interaction and shared public space

The Adda Experiment Re-imagines Public →

Spaces With Elements of Play →

The Adda Experiment is a social initiative by architects aiming to revitalize Indian urban spaces by incorporating play and engagement into public areas, especially for underserved communities.

Through community workshops and research, they address the scarcity of recreational spaces and explore how playful, inclusive designs can enhance urban wellbeing. Their work includes collaborative projects, such as those in Delhi, to create child-friendly environments and raise awareness of equitable public space access.

content_html:
In this edition

Editor's note U-CAN Initiatives Urban Climate Action U-CAN Member Highlight Mahila Housing Trust U-CAN Webinar Calendar of Upcoming Events

Editor's Note

As 2024 draws to a close, I take a moment to reflect upon the progress we have made, in this last newsletter for 2024. Our policy webinar series delved into complex issues that plague our cities.

We were able to succesfully launch our Fellowship this year and we are able to place highly capable fellows in our member organisations. We are keen to follow and share the work that our fellows will undertake over the next year. Our website and social media handle on Linkedin was launched in 2024 where the urban community have followed and embraced our purpose, vision and our work. We have started to present our network at various external engagements and we are highly encouraged to know that many organisations have expressed the need for a network like U- CAN that can bring leaders from the urban sector together and build bridges across the organisations. The member organisations continue to support us in our ambitions and the team has worked hard to begin turning the ambitions into reality.

We express our gratitude to all in helping us to build this network and we promise to come back in 2025 with a renewed sense of our purpose. Wishing you a happy, peaceful end to 2024.

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

U-CAN Initiatives

Fellowship Inauguration

U-CAN inaugurated its fellowship for an all women mid-career and social entrepreneur cohort this month. We were privileged to have Dr. Anita Patil Deshmukh, Executive Director of Partners for Urban Knowledge, Action and Research (PUKAR) as the keynote speaker.

Dr. Anita recalled interesting anecdotes from decades of rich experience and left the audience with nuggets of wisdom on working with marginalised communities in urban areas.

PUKAR is a Mumbai-based organization that champions the production of actionable research by urban communities who benefit from it. It was in the fitness of things that an inspirational women leader, who has been at the forefront of promoting community involvement in urban transformation, inaugurated our all-woman cohort of future urban leaders.

Fellowship Induction Training

This past month, we even brought our fellowship cohort together to spend two immersive days of getting to know each other, co-creating a plan for the year, and visualising how we can realise our hopes and transcend fears by working together towards a common goal. The two-day induction workshop also saw six of our member organisations that are hosting the fellows inspire us with their impact stories. The time spent in deep conversations and reflections has nudged us in the direction of finding a shared purpose and set us up really well for an exciting year-long fellowship journey.

Urban Climate Action

Indian cities are at the forefront of the climate crisis, grappling with challenges such as rising temperatures, increased urban flooding, and deteriorating air quality. As hubs of economic activity and home to a growing majority of the population, cities contribute significantly to carbon emissions but also hold immense potential for driving climate solutions. While urban India has witnessed promising initiatives, including the adoption of renewable energy, green buildings, and low-carbon mobility systems, the issue of climate action or climate change is a lot more complex. This compendium by WWF India guides you through various aspects of climate change at a global and national level, especially impacts on our cities.

Read More →

A snapshot of urban green finance in two Indian cities: Case studies of Hyderabad and Kolkata

Indian cities like Hyderabad and Kolkata face climate and population pressures, necessitating innovative green financing for resilient infrastructure. The report from The Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance outlines how both cities manage green finance flows across climate-related sectors, despite governance and funding challenges. Hyderabad has implemented renewable energy and waste initiatives but struggles with complex governance layers, while Kolkata sees success in low-carbon transport but needs better governance integration and funding access.

Click on the image above to read more.

From reviving traditional crops to climate-proofing infrastructure: How 5 Indian communities are adapting to climate change

Amidst increasing climate shocks like extreme weather events, grassroots communities are leading adaptation efforts with nature-based solutions, traditional practices, and local collaborations. Stories from regions like Kerala, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Odisha, and Mumbai showcase resilience through initiatives such as flood-proofing infrastructure, drought adaptation, rainwater harvesting, traditional crop revival, and community-led disaster preparedness, emphasizing the need for collective action and climate-resilient infrastructure.

Read More →

EPIC engages leading Indian experts as first ‘Clean Air Champions’ to strengthen localised air quality efforts

EPIC - The Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) has launched the Clean Air Champions, an advisory group of Indian experts, to provide localised insights and amplify its efforts to improve air quality. This group will support EPIC’s flagship Air Quality Life Index (AQLI), which links air pollution to life expectancy, and advance data-driven solutions for cleaner air.

Comprising leaders from diverse fields, the Champions aim to drive policy changes and public awareness in India, with plans to expand to other polluted regions globally.

Read More →

Climate Change and Cities: Learning Series

WRI India's 10-part E-learning series, launched with MoHUA, NIUA, alliance partners, and city authorities, aims to enhance cities' understanding of climate change and their role in driving climate action through policies, programs, and projects. It fosters peer learning, expert engagement, and opportunities for long-term collaborations to advance urban climate initiatives across India.

Click on the image above to read more.

Suggested readings on Urban Climate Action

Clmate Risk Atlas - India Climate →

Collaborative →

The Climate Risk Atlas by CEEW is a comprehensive toolkit aimed at mapping local climate vulnerabilities across India to support informed decision-making and build resilience.

Launched in 2020, it leverages tools like the Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) to assess district-level risks from floods, droughts, and cyclones, revealing that 75% of districts face extreme weather hotspots. The Atlas has influenced state-level climate action plans, including Maharashtra's, and piloted initiatives like heat action plans in Thane and capacity- building in Rajasthan.

Climate action plans for India’s emerging →

cities →

The article discusses the critical role of climate action plans (CAPs) in building resilient cities amidst rapid urbanization and escalating climate challenges in India. It highlights the example of Mira Bhayandar, a city implementing a CAP under the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat’s Urban Habitat Risk Resilience programme. CAPs involve steps like assessing climate risks, establishing greenhouse gas (GHG) baselines, and planning inclusive strategies for mitigation and adaptation. Key success factors include integrating resilience into early city development, leveraging open spaces for sustainable solutions, stakeholder engagement, and securing funding. Effective CAPs can transform urban centers into models of sustainability and climate preparedness.

Navigating India’s Climate Future Climate projections for India (2021 — 2040)*

Azim Premji University has curated high-

resolution climate projections for India, using CMIP6 data, offering detailed insights into the country's changing climate at a 25x25 km scale, aiding stakeholders in developing targeted resilience strategies. They emphasise the urgency of addressing a 1.5°C global temperature rise, which threatens India's ecosystems, agriculture, economy, and public health, underscoring the critical need for localised adaptation and mitigation efforts.

Click on the images above to read more.

climate change, its historical impacts, and how climate stresses affect local livelihoods. Through hands-on activities and root cause analysis, participants identified key climate challenges in their area and worked together to find solutions to strengthen their community’s resilience.

C40 Cities →

The C40 Cities Climate Action Guideis your go- →

to playbook for designing cities that are greener, →

resilient, and future-ready. Think compact, vibrant neighbuorhoods with bustling streets for people— not just cars. Envision renewable energy hubs, lush green spaces soaking up carbon, and climate solutions that lift everyone, especially vulnerable communities. Collaboration and creativity can transform urban landscapes into climate champions! Dive into these powerful strategies and be the change for our cities' sustainable future.

U-CAN conducted a webinar on Understanding Urban Climate Action in India on 22 November, 2024 with Jaya Dhindaw from WRI India and Shruti Narayan from C40 Cities.The session explored why urban centers are essential players in addressing climate challenges, while identifying the key stakeholders driving these efforts, and unpacking the significant barriers they encounter along the way.

Editor's Note

Hello and welcome to the first edition of this newsletter in 2025! This year, we’re scaling up our initiatives—from the fellowship to our webinar series—while driving forward key program priorities.

It’s been a busy but exciting start, fueled by persistence and a renewed commitment to building something meaningful for the urban sector.

So, what are we looking forward to in 2025? Our first program priority is our Small Grants Initiative which we have intentionally named Request for Collaboration. At U-CAN, we’ve spent and we continue to spend a considerable amount of time thinking about the big C - collaboration. What does it mean for organisations working within the urban sector to collaborate? What form does this collaboration take? What drives organisations to want to collaborate with others? These and many more questions are those we have thought of, reflected upon and discussed with others within our network. What we have also seen is that collaborations between organisations have immense potential to view urban challenges through a multi-sectoral and intersectional lens, especially when the people involved bring complementary skills and perspectives to the table. Keeping this in mind and after many months of work on designing our Small Grants Initiative, we’ll be launching it for our member organisations in February. Our goal under this initiative is to experiment with and learn from bold and radical ideas that push the boundaries of traditional partnerships and work being done in the urban sector.

Second, our core mission is to bring organisations together and spark collaboration. We plan to organise in-person convenings in three cities - Delhi, Bangalore and Mumbai, as well as online convenings which will involve innovative ways of problem-solving for urban challenges. We will be spending the next few weeks in building these convenings with our members, and we'd love to hear from you if you have any ideas!

Given the scaling of our programs and operations, we are also thinking about how we can reach out to more audiences through our communications, including this newsletter. As you may have noticed, we have reimagined the content and design of this newsletter, with the aim of providing a roundup of what's happening in our cities, highlighting the incredible work of our members, and including interesting and engaging factoids and resources about urban India. This is a learning journey for us, and as always, feel free to write back to us with your feedback, suggestions and recommendations!

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

State of our Cities

India’s urban landscape is complex, and understanding it requires access to diverse knowledge resources. Fortunately, several platforms offer rich insights - from NITI Aayog's Urbanisation

Knowledge Hub, the many reports by organisations like Janaagraha, Praja and WRI. These →

resources help us analyse urban challenges and drive informed action. Explore these sections to know more!

As part of their work on heat action in cities, Mahila Housing Trust is extending its greening efforts under Jodhpur’s Heat Action Plan. They’ve planted 1700+ saplings of native trees including Kaner, Khari Badam and Gulmohar - chosen due to their adaptability to the local context of Jodhpur.

eGov Foundation’s Viraj Tyagi shares his thoughts on why solving complex wicked problems →

requires investing time in co-creating ecosystems where collaboration drives impact. →

The second cohort of Reap Benefit’s Changemaker Fundees - young guns making a serious dent →

in civic and climate challenges across India - was announced. Funding is a common challenge across the change-making ecosystem. The Changemaker Fund bridges this gap, supporting young people who are ready to tackle challenges in their communities, but need a boost to turn their bold ideas into action.

The number of digital payments users from urban areas in India is 64% according to a report by TransUnion CIBIL and endorsed by the Reserve Bank of India’s Currency and Finance Report in 2024. While the share of rural users is witnessing a faster uptake in terms of new unique users, the market is currently dominated by users in urban and peri-urban areas.

India’s digital payments infrastructure, led by the Unified Payments Interface, has also expanded to countries beyond India, while the Indian government is working with many other governments to expand this list even further. India’s rapidly expanding digital payment ecosystem is an example of how Digital Public Infrastructure can rapidly transform a sector. To understand how DPI systems

work, watch our most recent webinar with Gautham Ravichander from eGov Foundation and →

Sridhar Ganapathy from Artha Global. →

Across three books, Kaveri unravels crimes in a city teeming with colonial-era intrigue—be it a glamorous theater, a bustling market, or the tranquil but deceptive lakesides. Each mystery is richly woven with history, culture, and social change, offering a vivid portrait of Bangalore’s past. Whether you’re a history enthusiast or a detective fiction fan, this series is a captivating journey into the city’s hidden stories!

Editor's Note

In mid-2024, we began thinking about ways to put out our way of thinking at U-CAN and our member organisations, about how we see cities, the challenges they face and the solutions we are collectively working on. One of the challenges in doing so was to reach an audience which is not already part of the urban ecosystem - students, young professionals, social innovators and partnership with Josh Talks, with whom U-CAN has created a four-part series of podcasts which were released this month.

The focus of the podcast series is to build a narrative of urban India by breaking down complex urban challenges to a younger audience, with the aim of driving citizen engagement through increased awareness of urban challenges and solutions. To this end, the series features prominent voices and experts in the urban sector, who talk about their journeys, and a variety of urban challenges our cities face today.

The first episode has Milind and Shruti talking about how urban challenges are a symptom of a larger problem of lack of planning and vision for our cities, and these can be addressed through evidence-based decision-making, being active citizens ourselves, and to understand the intersectionality of urban challenges. In episode two, I'm joined by Gautham where we talk about how growing up in cities have shaped our thought process, looking at cities as complex systems, and fundamentally changing how cities are planned and urban challenges are approached. In the next episode, Shilpa and Krishnan talk about the different roles played by different kinds of capital in urban problem solving, inclusive and participatory urban governance, and budgeting at the local government level. In the final episode (due to be released this weekend), Jagan and Anuj share their stories on why they work in the urban sector, the role of philanthropy in this space, and their ideas on getting more young people involved in our cities.

Each of these conversations have been carefully designed to bring out the expertise of the guests in a way such that it appeals to the audience, and we'd love to hear what you thought about the podcast series!

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

State of our Cities

The annual budget was presented by the Government of India earlier this month. As always, it created a lot of buzz around how the government is allocating resources. Praja Foundation put out a summary of what the budget has in store for our cities across sectors and decoding allocations for various initiatives, while Janaagraha has a detailed analysis of allocations for the urban sector.

This number is higher at 54.2% households owning bicycles and just 4.4% households owning cars in rural areas. In Chai, Chai, Bishwanath Ghosh embarks on an unusual journey to explore India’s overlooked railway junction towns—places where trains pause, but passengers rarely disembark. From Mughal Sarai to Jolarpettai, these in-between spaces unfold as characters in their own right, brimming with untold stories, lingering nostalgia, and quiet charm. In the first newsletter of 2025, we told you about our plan for the year with our Request for Collaboration, U-CAN’s Small Grants Initiative, as a key priority. The idea behind this initiative is to enable collaboration between our member organisations, and in keeping with that spirit, we designed it with collaboration at its core – incorporating member feedback at several stages. We launched the initiative as planned in February and are now at an advanced stage of selection, with our expert jury reviewing proposals for the grant. We will share more updates in next month's newsletter.

Our fellowship program is progressing well as we approach the half-year mark. A key component is the professional development of our fellows. As with our other programs, we spoke to the fellows in the initial weeks to understand the skills and knowledge they require to grow as leaders in the urban sector. Keeping their inputs in mind, we introduced fortnightly sessions in two formats:

  • Masterclasses by external experts on engaging topics such as workplace storytelling, urban governance structures, and critical thinking. More sessions are in the pipeline, including potential ones led by our member organisations.
  • Peer-to-peer learning sessions where fellows exchange experiences, best practices, and diverse perspectives in a collaborative environment.

These sessions have been highly engaging and well-received by our fellows, enriching their experience. We'd love to hear if you have any ideas on sessions that we could potentially hold for our fellows!

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

State of our Cities

A new study by the Sustainable Futures Collaborative assessed the implementation of extreme heat policies and actions across multiple cities in India, the first in a multi-part series. They conducted 88 interviews with city, district, and state government officials from disaster management, health, city planning, and labour departments, who are implementing heat actions in the selected nine cities. These cities were chosen for their high vulnerability to rising extreme heat events.

The report highlights that short-term actions such as providing drinking water, changing work schedules, and boosting hospital capacity before or during a heat wave, are driven by emergency directives from higher levels of government. However, city-level Heat Action Plans, which are meant to be long-term strategies, often have a weaker effect on policy due to weak institutionalisation.

The report also compiled responses based on the interviews to highlight the barriers to heat action in our cities. It concludes with recommendations focusing on capacity building, institutional support, and technology-driven solutions.

Mumbai is more than a backdrop—it’s an imposing presence. Its crowded streets, local trains, and distant city lights echo the protagonist’s solitude and unfulfilled dreams. With haunting ghazals like Seene Mein Jalan and Aap Ki Yaad Aati Rahi, Gaman is a lyrical, melancholic ode to urban migrants.

masthead_sub: April is upon us. The temperatures have soared across the country, and so has the action at U- CAN.
content_html:
In this edition

Editor's note Fellowship Corner State of our Cities Member Highlights Metro Metrics Library

Editor's Note

April is upon us. The temperatures have soared across the country, and so has the action at U- CAN. We recently awarded the inaugural Request for Collaboration (RFC) grant and hosted City Mixers in Bangalore and Mumbai with our member organizations.

Through these initiatives, we’re deepening collaboration — one through a formal, funded partnership between the winning organizations of the RFC grant, and the other through an evening of conversation about issues that matter to us, away from the pressures of work, deadlines, and the constructs of impact and scale. One effort aims to leverage each other’s organizational strengths; the other helps us understand each other’s motivation and alignment with the urban cause as individuals. Both show great promise — we’ll have to wait and see how they unfold.

A little more on the RFC: it was designed to help members address shared challenges in their work. Leading up to the deadline, we engaged closely with several member organizations. Many expressed strong interest and contributed thoughtful collaboration ideas. While the final proposals were few, each reflected care, creativity, and a spirit of openness. That members took the time to engage — through conversations, writing, and sharing — signals a collective desire to work more ambitiously and in concert.

One project team has now been selected for a nine-month pilot. U-CAN will support and document their journey, learning from every twist and turn.

Our City Mixers, hosted by WRI India in Bangalore and Artha Global in Mumbai, brought U-CAN members together in person for the very first time. The conversations were lively, thought- provoking, and full of potential — thanks in no small part to the champions who helped shape the discussions. In Bangalore, Dr. Siji Chacko (Jan Sahas) spotlighted migrant workers’ role in climate resilience. In Mumbai, Dr. Anita Patil-Deshmukh (PUKAR) led a rich dialogue on participatory research, with reflections from colleagues at Praja Foundation, Shelter Associates, and more.

There’s palpable energy for deeper, more honest learning across this collective. These mixers are now a monthly space, and we’re excited to see where they lead. As always, we’d love to hear from you — what resonated, what you’d like to see more of, and how we can make these gatherings even more meaningful.

And yes — please stay hydrated, and keep your pets hydrated too!

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

Fellowship Corner

Masterclass Recap:

On April 25, fellows participated in a session titled "Urban Planning in India" led by Dr. Champaka Rajagopal from CPR. The session offered valuable insights into the evolving landscape of urban planning in India and its future challenges.

Fellows’ Blogs

Our fellows have been sharing their insights through their blogs! In this edition, we’re featuring two of them:

Click on the images above to read each blog, and stay tuned for more insights from our fellows in upcoming editions!

State of our Cities

With over 1.1 billion people living in

informal settlements globally, it’s clear

that addressing informality requires those

most affected to be at the heart of the →

solution. A new collection of 14 case →

studies, published by GIZ in collaboration with Slum Dwellers International (SDI) and the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED), showcases just that—powerful, community-led approaches to urban innovation.

One standout case comes from India: The ROOH campaign supports low-income communities in Indian cities by providing resilient, low-carbon, and affordable housing. Through 17 Learning Labs across nine cities, women’s collectives have documented building materials, assessed vulnerabilities, and co-created climate-responsive housing solutions. For example, in Pimpri, Mahila Milan led efforts to retrofit roofs ahead of the monsoon, showcasing how local knowledge drives resilience, thus proving that informal settlements are not just vulnerable; they are hubs of innovation and action.

Member Highlights

Sparking youth civic action with Reap Benefit

Over 300 young people gathered at Bangalore

Creative Circus for a phone-free day filled with play, problem-solving, and civic innovation.

The sixth edition of SolveCon 2025, hosted

by Reap Benefit brought together 14 partner

organizations, offering hands-on, interactive experiences on climate action, local governance, and social justice.

Here’s what stood out:

  • Youth want to create, not just consume.
  • They’re looking for mentors who will walk with them through their journey.
  • They want relevance, challenge, and transformation—moving from apathy to action.
  • Digital-free spaces encourage deeper reflection and connection.
  • They’re already addressing climate, mobility, and governance issues at the neighborhood level.

Redefining urban living with Shelter Associates

Shelter Associates, in collaboration with Kolhapur Municipal Corporation and supported by the A.T.E. Chandra Foundation, recently hosted a workshop on Bondre Nagar, a pioneering community-led redevelopment project under PMAY-Urban. This project is the first in Maharashtra to achieve in-situ slum redevelopment under the Beneficiary-Led Construction (BLC) vertical of PMAY-Urban on government land. It’s a powerful example of how communities can lead their own housing transformation.

Key features of the Bondre Nagar model include:

  • Full slum redevelopment without relocation
  • Legal land rights secured for 77 households
  • Formation of a Cooperative Housing Society
  • Community-led design and decision-making
  • Strong partnerships between municipal corporations, NGOs, funders, and communities This innovative approach is already influencing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that could shape future PMAY policy and encourage scalable, replicable housing solutions across India.

Janaagraha on building urban futures

In Mint, Srikanth Viswanathan from Janaagraha argues that India’s cities need a complete governance overhaul. Despite big investments in housing and infrastructure, weak city systems, like delayed local elections and poor devolution of powers, are holding back real progress. He calls for three key reforms:

  • Empower local governments with real authority and resources
  • Build capacity in staffing, planning, and finance
  • Adopt place-based urban planning Without these changes, he says, India’s urban transformation will remain incomplete.

Metro Metrics

3.87 lakh

That’s the number of complaints Delhi citizens filed each year with the Municipal Corporation from 2017 to 2023 — more than 1,000 every single day. This figure comes from Praja Foundation’s latest Report on the Status of Wards Committees, which sheds light on functionality, citizen engagement, and accountability across the city’s 12 municipal zones.

So, what are the biggest concerns?

  • 42% Water supply
  • 27% sewerage
  • 26% Other issues
  • 5% Solid waste management The scale of complaints points to persistent service delivery gaps, and the urgent need for more responsive, ward-level governance.

Read the full report here →

Library

Looking for a book that will change the way you see cities—and maybe even yourself?

Invisible Cities by Italo Calvino is one we highly recommend.

Framed as an imagined conversation between the explorer Marco Polo and Emperor Kublai Khan, each chapter presents a city that is fantastical, poetic, and deeply metaphorical. These aren’t cities you’ll find on a map—they float, spiral, crumble, and shimmer with memory, desire, and imagination.

Calvino gently blurs the boundary between urban form and human experience, showing that cities are shaped not just by architecture, but by the people who dream, remember, and live within them. This isn’t just a book about cities; it’s a meditation on how we experience the world around us.

content_html:
In this edition

Editor's note State of our Cities Designing the collective: Reflections from Goa Member Highlights Fellowship Corner Metro Metrics! Library

Editor's Note

May brought the first rains, and a big moment for U-CAN. Earlier this month, we met with our members in person in Goa for our first Steering Committee meeting of 2025. More than just a catch-up, it was a space to connect, communicate, and collaborate - three anchors that are shaping how we move forward as a collective.

This gathering also came at a critical halfway point in our Fellowship journey. It gave members a chance to reflect on the value the program is generating, not just in terms of knowledge and capacity, but also in building relationships across the ecosystem. We asked the hard questions:

What does it really mean to put Tier II and III cities front and centre, not as smaller versions of metros, but as places with their own stories, challenges, and possibilities? How do we design structures that fosters real collaboration and sparks creativity? And how do we hold space for many voices yet maintain the amorphous nature of our network?

While we still figure it out, the signs are encouraging - the room was full of conversations, care, and commitment. This is especially important now, as we begin planning for U-CAN’s first annual forum in August and the work of building a common narrative for Tier II and III cities.

Below, you’ll find a snapshot of the conversations and the energy that made this gathering special.

Meanwhile, our U-CAN Fellows are out there writing fresh reflections from the ground, sharing what they’re learning as they work with partner organisations. These blogs offer a window into the realities of urban practitioners navigating complex city systems, and how their stories can sharpen our collective thinking.

As always, we’d love to hear what resonates with you, what you’re seeing in your own work, and how we can keep building this space together.

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

State of our Cities

Inequities in urban health: A growing crisis

A recent study by the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP) reveals widening health disparities in India’s urban areas - particularly affecting the urban poor. Despite improved national health indicators, the urban poor face significantly worse outcomes compared to both rural populations and the urban non-poor.

Drawing on data from the National Sample Survey (NSS), National Family Health Survey (NFHS), Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI), and government health statistics, the study finds that urban health outcomes are increasingly shaped by structural determinants, such as inadequate housing, poor sanitation, and limited access to essential public services. Despite higher aggregate availability of health infrastructure in cities, intra-urban inequities persist, with the urban poor often relying on costly private care due to the uneven distribution and perceived quality gaps in public facilities. Finally, initiatives like the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) have struggled due to underfunding and fragmented governance.

The report calls for urgent reforms, including better NUHM implementation, increased funding, and a unified urban health governance body, to prevent deepening disparities and ensure equitable health access for all urban residents.

Uncover the Insights →

Designing the collective: Reflections from Goa

Earlier this month, U-CAN’s Steering Committee gathered in Goa for a milestone in our collective journey - our first in-person meeting of 2025. Over two days, we engaged in focused discussions that moved beyond routine updates to tackle fundamental questions about collaboration and collective action.

The sessions challenged us to rethink what it takes to build meaningful partnerships across cities, especially India’s Tier II and III urban centers. How can we foster environments that encourage experimentation, mutual support, and care, rather than just coordination? What would it look like to centre these cities on their own terms and priorities?

Through a mix of facilitated conversations, group reflections, and creative exercises, members surfaced both big-picture aspirations and practical challenges. We revisited U-CAN’s shared vision, examined current initiatives, and laid groundwork for the next phase of our collective work.

A key focus was planning for U-CAN’s first annual forum and shaping a narrative for tier II and III cities in India that can guide our efforts. The meeting ended on a note of optimism and commitment, with participants energized by new ideas and strengthened connections. Alongside this momentum, we also took time to celebrate the creative spirit of the group - hand-painted magnets were a small but meaningful reminder of the care and collaboration we aim to cultivate moving forward.

Member Highlights

WRI India rethinks cities through the eyes of women caregivers

On Mother’s Day (May 11), WRI India reminded us that caregiving is a full-time, year-round responsibility - especially for women who often navigate cities not designed with their needs in mind.

In a recent blog, Madhura Kulkarni and Chaitali Patil explore how caregiving burdens impact women’s well-being and workforce participation—and why caregiver-friendly urban design is essential for building inclusive, equitable cities.

Through the #NurturingNeighbourhoods initiative, WRI India is working with cities to make this vision a reality.

Read the blog here →

Civic Services in Mumbai: What Praja’s 2025 Report Reveals

Praja Foundation’s latest annual report, The Status of Civic Issues in Mumbai, offers a sobering assessment of the city’s core public services. Despite Mumbai’s sizable municipal budget, systemic shortfalls persist—especially for slum communities and the urban poor. Here are some key takeaways:

  • Water: A 15% shortfall in daily supply; only 8% of residents have 24/7 access. Slum communities are hit hardest.
  • Sewage: Most sewage treatment plants fail to meet pollution norms. The Mithi River remains dangerously contaminated.
  • Toilets: Just 1 public seat per 1,820 women—many lack access to basic water and power.
  • Waste: The city generated 6,656 MTD of waste in 2024, a 4% increase since 2022.
  • Compliance: 64% of bulk waste generators are not treating wet waste on-site.
  • Costs: Waste transport and processing cost the city ₹1,485 crore in 2024.
  • Landfills: Biomining at Mulund landfill is behind schedule, with a June 2025 deadline looming.
  • Air Quality: Slight gains—2024 saw four “moderate” AQI months, compared to six in 2023.
  • Citizen Complaints: Over 1.15 lakh grievances filed in 2024—primarily around waste, water, and toilets.
  • Staffing Gaps: 41% of BMC posts remain vacant—highest in Education (59%), Stormwater Drains (57%), and Roads (54%).

Praja’s findings underscore an urgent need to prioritize infrastructure upgrades, ensure equitable access to services, and address chronic staffing shortages across departments.

📖 Read the full report here →

Jodhpur gets cooler with Mahila Housing Trust's climate-responsive pilot.

Mahila Housing Trust (MHT) recently piloted India’s first Net-Zero Cooling Station in Jodhpur, as part of the city’s Heat Action Plan. The station is designed to offer accessible, energy- efficient heat relief in dense urban neighbourhoods, and is gaining recognition as a promising approach to urban heat resilience.

This pilot is now informing the development of national Cooling Station Guidelines, being shaped by National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI), the Natural Resources Defense Council (lNRDC), India, the Centre for Advanced Research in Building Science and Energy (CARBSE), and others. These guidelines are expected to support similar efforts across India and in other Least Developed Countries facing rising heat stress.

Rooted in MHT’s long-standing work on climate resilience in informal settlements, the initiative highlights how targeted, place-based interventions can help cities adapt to extreme heat.

Shelter Associates Turns 30!

Shelter Associates celebrates 30 years of empowering urban poor communities through data- driven, community-led solutions. From pioneering GIS-based slum mapping and providing digital addresses to 100,000+ households, to improving hygiene for over 200,000 people through the One Home One Toilet model, their work has consistently advanced dignity, inclusion, and public health.

Their approach, grounded in participatory housing design and evidence-based planning, has helped families access secure housing, shaped national policy, and fostered long-term change.

A remarkable milestone for an organisation reimagining urban development, one community at a time.

Read more about their journey →

Fellowship Corner

Building Urban Resilience from the Ground Up

What does it take to build cities that are climate-resilient and inclusive? That’s the question U-CAN Fellows explored in the first session of a three-part masterclass with Campaign for ROOH - a global initiative advancing community-led housing and public spaces.

Two inspiring voices led the session:

  • Sheela Patel (Founder, SPARC; Co-founder, SDI; currently with ROOH under the UN’s Race to Resilience) challenged prevailing narratives on informal settlements. Her message: These communities are not the problem; they are the solution.
  • Fellows reflected on climate vulnerabilities in their cities, and the urgent need for community-led resilience strategies rooted in lived experience.
  • Dr. Eleni (Lenio) Myrivili (Global Chief Heat Officer, UN-Habitat) spotlighted urban heat as a growing and unequal threat. Her reminder: “The story of heat is the story of inequality.”
  • Fellows discussed how design, infrastructure, and policy can mitigate heat stress - specially for the most vulnerable.

Explore the full Masterclass series to see what else Fellows are engaging with →

City, Self, and Systems: Reflections from the Fellowship

This month, we bring you more blogs from the Fellows — reflections that connect the personal with the political, the local with the systemic.

In A City I Knew, A Crisis I See, Sharathppriyaa Venkatesan reflects on Bengaluru’s changing climate and how it reveals deeper challenges in urban governance.

In Towards a More Democratic City, Aanchal Aggarwal shares insights from Jammu on why community participation is vital for city planning and inclusive governance.

In Between Heritage and Hangouts, U-CAN Fellow Aashima Arora explores how young people in Jaipur navigate the city’s historic charm amid a lack of safe, inclusive public spaces.

In Addressing Women’s Safety Challenges in Gurugram, Anwesha Bhattacharya examines rising gender-based safety issues and the need to challenge social norms alongside improving infrastructure.

📚 Click here to read all the blogs →

Metro Metrics!

That’s the percentage of India’s urban wastewater that is treated - meaning a huge 72% remains untreated and flows directly into rivers, lakes, and land.

A report from the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), Waste to Worth: Managing India’s urban water crisis through wastewater reuse, highlights this critical gap and the urgent opportunity it presents. With increasing water scarcity driven by rapid urbanisation, industrial growth, population pressure, and climate change, treating and reusing wastewater is key to creating a sustainable, circular water economy.

The Ministry of Jal Shakti has mandated that cities recycle and reuse at least 20% of the water they consume. Some states and cities are leading by example: Maharashtra requires industries to use treated wastewater; Gujarat aims for 100% reuse in agriculture and industry; Tamil Nadu promotes reuse for urban greening and industry. Cities such as Nagpur, Bengaluru, and Chennai have implemented innovative wastewater reuse projects, reducing freshwater demand in power generation, agriculture, and groundwater recharge.

Despite this progress, challenges like infrastructure gaps, water quality assurance, cultural resistance, and treatment costs continue to slow scale-up. The report calls for better policy alignment, investment in decentralised treatment technologies, public-private partnerships, and capacity building among urban officials and communities.

Library

What should a city built for working women look like?

In Feminist City: Claiming Space in the Man- Made World, geographer Leslie Kern challenges us to rethink how urban spaces are designed - and for whom.

She paints a picture of a city where public transit supports caregivers on the move, streets are safe to walk at all hours, toilets, green spaces, and care infrastructure are priorities - not afterthoughts - and many more!

Blending history, lived experience, and cultural critique, Kern exposes how gendered inequalities are built into our cities - and offers a vision for more just, inclusive, and care-full urban futures.

In this edition

Editor's note Grounding reform in voice and visibility: June steering committee takeaways State of our Cities Member Highlights Fellowship Corner Metro Metric Library

Editor's Note

Some of the most important shifts in urban governance happen through steady, behind-the-scenes work; in conversations, pilots, and quiet experiments that build over time. June gave us a glimpse of that across the U-CAN network.

At our virtual Steering Committee meeting, we paused to reflect on where we are and where we want to go. Members shared ideas to make U-CAN convenings more useful, from co-creating agendas to setting up more informal spaces for exchange. We also started a conversation on the kinds of stories we need to tell, especially those that highlight the work happening in Tier II and III cities.

This month’s updates show how that work is taking shape. In Kurukshetra, students led conversations on democracy and local government. In smaller cities across Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, municipal officials shared practical air quality solutions with each other through peer learning that cuts across state boundaries. Efforts to improve clean air in cities like Dhule, Latur, and Solapur are as urgent and complex as those in big metros, and deserve equal attention.

We also saw how ideas developed in larger cities like Mumbai and Chennai, such as climate budgeting and planning reforms, can offer useful lessons for smaller cities if adapted with care.

The goal is not to replicate but to translate what works into very different local contexts.

U-CAN Fellows and member organisations are at the heart of this work. Whether it’s water resilience, housing, or mapping informal settlements, they are showing what it takes to make systems more responsive, one neighbourhood, one pilot, and one dialogue at a time.

As we prepare for U-CAN’s first annual forum in August, this work helps ground us. Strong networks, like strong cities, take time. They grow through collaboration, trust, and a shared commitment to cities that are often overlooked but central to India’s urban future.

Siddharth Pandit

CEO, Urban Collective Action Network · On behalf of U-CAN

Grounding reform in voice and visibility: June steering committee takeaways

U-CAN’s mid-year Steering Committee check-in, held on June 18, focused on making our collective work more effective; starting with how we meet, plan, and tell stories. Members emphasized the need for convenings that are co-created, informal, and tailored to spark honest, grounded exchange. The goal: more meaningful conversations, better connections, and outcomes that carry forward.

We also reflected on U-CAN’s positioning. A proposal to frame the network as a platform for coordinated reform received strong interest, with members urging clarity around language, stakeholder engagement, and strategic alignment, especially in today’s policy environment.

Finally, we began shaping a clearer storytelling approach. Members underlined the need to move beyond metro-centric narratives and highlight the complexity, creativity, and leadership emerging from smaller cities. These are not scaled-down metros, they are dynamic systems in their own right.

With mixers, strategy meetings, and the Annual Forum around the corner, these insights will help ground the next phase of U-CAN’s journey.

State of our Cities

Good cities need good governance, not just big projects

Urban governance in India is at a tipping point. In his recent article “Why bigger may not be better for Indian cities”, Partha Mukhopadhyay, Senior Fellow at the Centre for Policy Research, critiques how political leaders across parties are approaching urbanisation. Rather than a cohesive strategy, what we often see is a patchwork of decisions shaped by short-term optics and fragmented priorities.

The article uses recent developments to illustrate this disconnect. The creation of the Greater Bengaluru Authority, which shifts power away from elected representatives to state-led control, reflects a growing trend toward administrative centralisation. At the same time, national investment plans like the Urban Challenge Fund and the ADB’s $10 billion urban program focus heavily on large metros, despite political messaging that highlights the importance of Tier II and III cities.

The article raises three critical questions:

1. Should we focus on big cities or smaller ones?

Large cities may produce more GDP, but they are also harder to govern and more vulnerable to rent-seeking. Smaller cities, with fewer entrenched interests, may be better positioned for meaningful reform.

2. Who governs our cities?

Models like the GBA may improve coordination but reduce democratic accountability. The article proposes a possible middle path: state control over capital cities, but full implementation of the 74th Amendment in other urban areas.

3. What defines a city?

As urban regions spill across municipal and even state boundaries, planning and governance need to shift from administrative lines to functional economic regions. Without this shift, city planning remains fragmented.

The article also critiques performative urban interventions, like Delhi’s mandate for anti-smog guns or costly metro systems that do little to solve mobility challenges. These projects may look modern, but they often lack real impact.

The author's central argument is clear: Before we invest in new infrastructure or announce bold reforms, we need to ask more fundamental questions about power, representation, and what it means to govern a city effectively.

📘Uncover the Insights →

Member Highlights

Mumbai’s climate budget links finance with equity, mobility, and livelihoods On World Environment Day (June 5), the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) released its second Climate Budget Report for FY 2025–26. This marks a significant step in how Indian cities can integrate climate goals into everyday governance, using public finance as a lever for systemic change.

This is more than a climate document. It reflects how urban budgets can address interconnected issues like flooding, air pollution, and heat stress, while also shaping how people live and move. By embedding climate action across sectors like transport, waste, and housing, the budget has implications for jobs, gender equity, and access to basic services. When mobility systems are made cleaner and more inclusive, or when waste systems are strengthened with safeguards for informal workers, climate action becomes social action too.

Rooted in the Mumbai Climate Action Plan (MCAP) and supported by U-CAN members C40 Cities and WRI India, the report brings together global frameworks and strong local ownership.

Why this matters:

  • This is India’s first structured and sustained effort to institutionalise climate budgeting
  • Climate goals are integrated into the budgets of core departments across six key sectors
  • Parastatal agencies like BEST are included, connecting climate finance with public transport and service delivery
  • A pilot Monitoring, Evaluation, and Reporting (MER) system strengthens accountability
  • Equity and resilience indicators help ensure climate investments work for women, informal workers, and other marginalised groups
  • Climate-aligned capital spending has increased to ₹16,321 crore, up from ₹10,224 crore last year
  • 739 climate-linked activities are being tracked, with 86.26% financial progress in FY 2024–25 Mumbai is showing what becomes possible when climate ambition is backed by institutional capacity and financial commitment. It sets an important precedent for cities across India and the Global South.

📘 Read the full report →

Democracy begins in the classroom: Young citizens take the lead in Kurukshetra On the 32nd anniversary of the 74th Constitutional Amendment - a landmark moment for decentralized urban governance - Janaagraha flipped the script.

This wasn’t just another policy dialogue. It was a glimpse into what participatory democracy can actually look like:

  • 150+ students from 20 government schools in Kurukshetra joined live, thanks to their Civic and Social Action Program (CSAP)
  • 200+ participants came together, from elected representatives and bureaucrats to researchers and grassroots activists
  • The discussion focused on power, participation, and youth agency, and what it really takes to shift governance closer to the people The big takeaway? Real change begins when young citizens are not just informed, but included.

And when classrooms become the training ground for democracy, the future of our cities looks a lot more hopeful.

Click on the link below to watch the full proceedings

Peer learning is powering clean air action across Indian cities

As cities across India grapple with the growing challenges of air pollution, peer learning is proving to be a powerful tool for action. This month, Artha Global’s Centre for Emerging Cities, in partnership with the Directorate of Municipal Administration, Government of Maharashtra, hosted a peer learning workshop focused on urban air quality management. The convening brought together over 35 municipal representatives from across Maharashtra, alongside partner cities from Andhra Pradesh.

Cities including Dhule, Akola, Latur, Mumbai, Pune, Solapur, and Thane shared practical solutions being implemented under the National Clean Air Programme; from mechanised road washing to emission control initiatives. Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada added insights from their work on Clean Air Zones, shaped through public transport upgrades and stakeholder engagement.

This workshop is part of Artha’s ongoing ‘Excellence in Urban Leadership’ programme, now in its third year, which aims to build the capacity of city leaders to create cleaner, healthier, and more resilient urban environments. This effort was also supported by U-CAN, as part of our shared commitment to enabling meaningful city-to-city learning.

Planning is climate action: Embedding resilience into the urban fabric Can urban planning fight climate change? That was the big question at a national conference hosted in Chennai on June 20 by C40 Cities and the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Lab.

From senior officials like Supriya Sahu and Nilesh Rajadhyaksha to leaders from the Tamil Nadu government and CMDA, the message was consistent: climate resilience starts on the drawing board.

What stood out:

  • Planning as a frontline tool for climate adaptation
  • Breaking silos through integrated governance
  • Rethinking land use, budgets, and priorities The event also saw the launch of a new Policy Note, offering a practical playbook for cities to embed climate into their master plans.

The takeaway? Climate-smart cities aren’t an add-on, they’re essential. And it all begins with how we plan.

More about the policy note in the next version of this newsletter!

Fellowship Corner

Water resilience through youth action: A spotlight from UrbanAdda

At UrbanAdda 2025 in New Delhi, Shubhi Kesarwani, Co-founder & CEO of GuruJal and U-CAN Fellow, led a compelling set of sessions spotlighting youth leadership in water resilience.

Hosted by GuruJal as part of the larger event organised by Raahgiri Foundation and International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), the Water Ambassador Award Ceremony honoured students from across India who conducted household water audits and led awareness efforts under the National Water Audit Survey.

Archana Varma, IAS, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Water Mission, delivered the keynote and launched the Rainwater Harvesting Calculator, developed by GuruJal, a new tool to support both individual and institutional recharge planning.

From championing youth to sparking systems conversations, it’s inspiring to see U-CAN Fellows like Shubhi shaping grounded, future-facing solutions, and bringing U-CAN’s collective vision to life!

Housing is not a service, it’s a right: Lessons in dignity, agency, and ownership from a

ROOH masterclass

What does it mean to truly see urban poor habitats, not as informal or temporary, but as homes, communities, and sites of resilience?

In the second session of the Roof Over Our Heads (ROOH) masterclass series on June 20, Fellows explored this question through powerful stories and grounded insights from Nairobi, Surat, and India’s ROOH Labs.

Christine and Pauline, grassroots leaders from Mukuru and Mathare in Nairobi, shared how their communities are mapping needs, shaping plans, and co-creating housing solutions with city governments. Their message was clear: collective agency is not just possible, it is already underway.

Smruti Jukur from SPARC introduced the ROOH framework, calling for a shift in how we think about housing for the urban poor. A short film from Surat offered a glimpse of what this looks like on the ground - homes built by communities that reflect their own aspirations.

The session closed with reflections from federation leader Bano Ansari and youth leaders Aryan, Sharmila, and Siddhi. They spoke candidly about lived challenges and shared how ownership, inclusion, and dignity are not abstract ideals but everyday practices.

Two sessions down, two more to go. The journey continues.

Explore the full Masterclass series to see what else Fellows are engaging with →

Metro Metric

68%

of dengue cases are urban. It’s time our response reflected that.

In 2024, India recorded over 2.3 lakh dengue cases; nearly a third of the global total. Strikingly, 68% of these were from urban areas, making it clear that dengue is not just a public health crisis. It is an urban crisis.

On World Dengue Day (June 15), the EquiHealth Alliance released a new outcomes paper, “Advancing Access and Strengthening Dengue Response,” launched by AVPN with ETI as technical partner. Drawing from work in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the report outlines a strategy that goes beyond treatment, focusing on prevention, data, and community engagement.

Why does this matter? Dengue outbreaks are shaped by more than viruses and vectors.

  • It’s a planning issue because poor waste management, stagnant water, and housing conditions in growing cities create the perfect environment for mosquito breeding.
  • It’s a climate issue because rising temperatures and erratic rainfall patterns are expanding the window for transmission.
  • It’s a governance issue because effective prevention depends on how departments coordinate, how quickly data moves, and how well local systems respond.

From building early warning systems to supporting behaviour change, the report shows that dengue control needs more than medicine. It needs cities that are designed to prevent it in the first place.

📖Read the full report here →

Library

Repair is climate action - we just don’t see it that way

E‑waste is the world’s fastest-growing waste stream, expected to hit 82 million metric tons by 2030, far outpacing recycling efforts. But what if we stopped seeing discarded electronics as waste, and started recognising the environmental labour of repair?

In this feature, Dr. Julia Corwin (London School of Economics) shares insights from nearly two years of fieldwork in Delhi’s repair hubs. Her upcoming book, Analog Labour in a Digital World, reframes repair as a form of care and climate stewardship, not just convenience.

Dr Corwin argues that electronics repair and reuse should be recognised as “labour that is doing significant environmental work but is not often given environmental attention.”
